title: Breathing, read whole
hookLine: the sixteen steps fulfill the four foundations and the seven factors

lines: ONE BREATH. THREE. LONG AND SHORT.
cards: You've met the breath on this path many times: one breath with the bell, three breaths, long and short. Pieces. Today, the whole thing.

The hundred and eighteenth discourse is set at the Eastern Park near Savatthi. The rains retreat should be ending, but the Buddha is so pleased with his monks that he stays another month, until the next full moon.
New monks arrive to learn, and senior monks teach them, ten, twenty, thirty, forty students each. And on that full-moon night, the Buddha teaches mindfulness of breathing from start to finish.

teach.b: It's called anapanasati: mindfulness of in-breath and out-breath. You go to a forest, the root of a tree or an empty hut, sit with the body upright, and set mindfulness in front of you.
Then come sixteen steps, in four sets of four. The first four are the body. Breathing in long, you know it's long; breathing in short, you know it's short.
You train to breathe in experiencing the whole body, and calming the body. The second four are feeling: breathing with joy, with ease, knowing how feelings shape the mind, and calming that.
The third four are the mind: knowing it, gladdening it, steadying it, releasing it. The last four are what you see: impermanence, fading, ending, letting go. Then the big claim.
These sixteen steps, the Buddha says, fulfill the four foundations of mindfulness, body, feeling, mind and phenomena, one set of four each.

The four foundations, practiced well, fulfill the seven factors of awakening: mindfulness, investigation, energy, joy, calm, concentration and equanimity. And those seven, fulfilled, bring true knowledge and release.
One breath, followed all the way, carries the entire path. That's a big promise about something you do some twenty thousand times a day without noticing. Nothing in it needs a special tool.

how: Mindfulness of breathing is one of the most widely taught meditations across Theravada, Zen and Tibetan schools, and many teachers lead students through the sixteen steps of MN 118, often over weeks of retreat.

he remains until the full moon of the next month, and new monks come to learn.

the sixteen steps move through body, feeling, mind and phenomena.

games.q: you've known long and short breaths. what's the third step of the sixteen?
o: breathe in experiencing the whole body.
stop breathing to test the mind.
games.why: step three is breathing in and out experiencing the whole body; step four is calming it.

practice: Sit upright: breathing in long, know it's long; breathing in short, know it's short. Then breathe in and out feeling the whole body, and if it settles, let each in-breath calm the body a little more.
